sentences.text: said it better than I did there.
I don't think so.
I'm just excited.
So how does training a crew for Artemis differ than training a crew for the space station,
besides, you know, the fact that it's Orion and maybe the moon, things like that?
Yeah, I think the biggest difference to me is that for Orion, we're still developing
the ops concepts, the hardware, the vehicle is still being developed while we're doing
the training.
So for ISS, the mission is pretty set when you start training.
You know roughly what you need to do and some of the experiments that will be on board,
and you can really train towards that.
For Orion, the mission is set, but the timeline is still up in the air, and the ops concepts,
they're still being developed while we're training.
So you really have to focus on general skills and vehicle knowledge so that it can all come
together in the 11th hour when everything's been decided and you know exactly what the
mission is going to be.
That's a great point.
I mean, versus we've had people flying on the space station coming up for 26 continuous
years now, and so that is quite a drastic difference versus one space flight of humans
on Orion for 10 days.
So very, very, very good point on we're building it as it's being flown.
What is something that the public might be surprised to learn about from astronaut training
for Artemis missions?
I think the most surprising thing is how little of our training I want them to use in flight.
That's a good point.
Like we spend most of our time training worst case scenarios, different failure things that
could go wrong, and ideally nothing.
Yeah.
I mean, the most phenomenal happens during the mission.
But by practicing all of those failures, they're learning the process, they're working as a
team.
There's a lot of skills that are applicable, but the exact scenarios we train, I hope they
never use it.
Yeah.
No, that's a great point because I mean, there's so much work that goes into preventing a really
bad day and preparing for a really bad day.
And everybody's hope is that, "Hey, I'm working on this thing that you never touch or that
you never have to call to mind," which is such a funny thing, but it gives people peace
of mind.
And it gives you confidence in the mission and it gives the crew confidence in the spacecraft
and the ground teams knowing that every single little item has been worked through.
That's a very, very funny and great point, hoping that they never have to call back what
it's like to execute a fire response or something like that.
Yep, exactly.
Tell me about training so far.
Is there a moment that has stood out to you just in some way?
If it's good, if it's challenging, anything unexpected yet?
What stood out the most was actually last week, we got the crew all suited up and we
put them in the capsule like it was the day of launch and we walked and talked through
some things, but just watching them on the video feed, all four of them in there all
suited up, it felt real.
It felt like watching Artemis II crew on launch day.
So that's when I first got the goosebumps and I'm like, "This is really happening.
This is real.
This is what it's going to feel like on launch day."
So I mean, that was just an exciting moment.
It's so cool.
I see it in my mind, kind of like those scenes in a movie where you're watching something
in real time, but then you flash forward to what's coming up and then it's launch day
all of a sudden and you flash back to that moment.
I don't know if that's real.
Exactly.
I went into mom mode.
And I'm like, "I'm going to take pictures."
Good.
I'm sure they all appreciate that and you'll thank yourself too when they launch next year.
So talking about training, you were saying earlier how it's part of your job to make
sure everyone is totally finalized in what they need to know.
How do you know when, what officially marks the end of training?
How do you know that they are ready to go fly the spacecraft?
That's a great question.
You really know once you get in a sim and you just see the entire team, not just the
crew, but the entire team working together well.
And we won't have everything perfected and nailed down just perfect.
But when we get to a point where we are solving problems together and we're doing it in a
timely fashion, you see that transition and you know you're ready.
